This page runs R inside your browser. It needs about 22 MB on first load — the

Almost everything you will do to a table on Day 1 is one of five verbs: keep
some **rows** (`filter()`), keep some **columns** (`select()`), reorder rows
(`arrange()`), add a column (`mutate()`), and collapse many rows into a summary
(`summarise()`). Learn these five and you can do real work.

From here on you are working with the actual workshop cohort — the same 240
synthetic students the 11:15 session on Day 1 uses. By the time you sit down in
the room, this file will already be familiar. For the full explanation of any of
this, see [the R primer](r-primer.qmd).

## Reading the data

`read_csv()` comes from **readr**. It takes a path to a file and gives you back
a tibble. `glimpse()` from dplyr turns that tibble on its side so you can see
every column at once — the right first move with any new dataset.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

students <- read_csv("data/meded_students.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(students)
```

240 rows, 17 columns. Read the type tags down the left: `<chr>` is text,
`<dbl>` is a number with decimals. Note that `batch` is a `<dbl>` — R read
`2024` as a number, not as a label, so you write `batch == 2024` without
quotation marks.

The same line works unchanged in RStudio on Day 1, because your project will
have a `data/` folder holding the same file. That is the whole point of the
`data/meded_students.csv` path: it is relative to your project, not to your
computer, so the script runs on anyone's machine.

::: {.callout-warning title="One way this browser lies to you"}
The file arrived here by magic — this page downloaded it for you. In RStudio
you will put the file in your project's `data/` folder yourself. The
`library()` calls are the same magic in reverse: already run for you here,
essential at the top of every script there. Type them anyway.
:::

## `filter()` — keep some rows

`filter()` keeps the rows where a condition is `TRUE` and drops the rest.

```{webr}
students |>
  filter(teaching_arm == "Flipped classroom")
```

120 of the 240 students. Note the **double** equals sign: `==` asks a question,
`=` assigns a value. Using `=` here is one of the two or three most common
beginner errors in R.

## `select()` — keep some columns

`select()` does for columns what `filter()` does for rows. Name the ones you
want, in the order you want them.

```{webr}
students |>
  select(student_id, batch, pretest, posttest, gain)
```

Seventeen columns is more than you can read at once. Selecting five of them is
often the difference between seeing your data and squinting at it.

## `arrange()` — reorder the rows

`arrange()` sorts. It sorts ascending by default; wrap the column in `desc()`
for descending.

```{webr}
students |>
  arrange(desc(burnout_score)) |>
  select(student_id, college, burnout_score)
```

Student S133 has the highest burnout score at 87.5. Sorting is how you find the
extremes — the highest, the lowest, the implausible value that turns out to be a
data-entry slip.

## `mutate()` — add a column

`mutate()` adds a new column computed from existing ones. It never removes
anything.

```{webr}
students |>
  mutate(gain_check = posttest - pretest) |>
  select(student_id, pretest, posttest, gain, gain_check)
```

`gain_check` reproduces the `gain` column, which is a cheap way to confirm you
have understood what a column means.

Look at row 3. `posttest` is `NA` — R's marker for *missing* — and so
`gain_check` is `NA` too. Arithmetic on an unknown value gives an unknown
answer. Eleven students in this cohort have no posttest score, which is exactly
what real data looks like, and it will bite you in Exercise 2.

## `summarise()` — collapse rows into a summary

`summarise()` reduces many rows to one. Paired with `group_by()`, it reduces
many rows to one **per group** — which is most of what a results table is.

```{webr}
students |>
  group_by(batch) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_attendance = round(mean(attendance_pct), 1)
  )
```

Three batches, three rows. `n()` counts the rows in each group; always report it
alongside a mean, so your reader knows whether that mean rests on 8 students or
80.

We spell it `summarise`. dplyr also accepts `summarize` — the two are the same
function, so use whichever spelling you prefer and be consistent.

## Putting them together

The verbs are designed to be chained. This is where Primer 3's pipe pays off:
read it as a sentence — *take the students, keep the 2024 batch, keep four
columns, sort by attendance, highest first*.

```{webr}
students |>
  filter(batch == 2024) |>
  select(student_id, college, attendance_pct, posttest) |>
  arrange(desc(attendance_pct))
```

Each verb does one small thing. The pipeline does something useful. Note that
`students` itself is untouched — dplyr verbs return a new table rather than
editing the old one, so you can experiment freely.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise:
#|   - ex_filter
#|   - ex_group
#|   - ex_college
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

students <- read_csv("data/meded_students.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: two conditions at once"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Keep only the students in the **2024 batch** whose `attendance_pct` is
**above 85**. Both conditions must hold.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_filter
students |>
  ______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_filter
#| solution: true
students |>
  filter(batch == 2024, attendance_pct > 85)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_filter
#| check: true
expected_ids <- students |>
  dplyr::filter(batch == "2024", attendance_pct > 85) |>
  dplyr::pull(student_id) |>
  sort()
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "filter() returns a table. Did you pipe into it?")
} else if (identical(sort(.result$student_id), expected_ids)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Check both conditions: batch == \"2024\" AND attendance_pct > 85.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_filter"}
One `filter()`, two conditions, separated by a comma — a comma inside
`filter()` means AND. `batch` is a number here, so no quotation marks are
needed around `2024`.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: mean posttest by teaching arm"}
**Time:** 10 minutes

Produce one row per `teaching_arm` showing the number of students and their
mean `posttest` score. Call the columns `n` and `mean_posttest`.

Remember the eleven missing posttest scores. `mean()` of anything containing an
`NA` is `NA` — try it without a guard first and see what comes back.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_group
students |>
  group_by(______) |>
  summarise(
    n = ______,
    mean_posttest = ______
  )
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_group
#| solution: true
students |>
  group_by(teaching_arm) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_posttest = mean(posttest, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_group
#| check: true
target <- sort(c(76.42478, 70.71034))
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "summarise() returns a table. Start from students and pipe into group_by() then summarise().")
} else if (!("teaching_arm" %in% names(.result)) || nrow(.result) != 2) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Expected one row per teaching arm, and there are two arms. Did you group_by(teaching_arm) before summarising?")
} else {
  nums <- Filter(is.numeric, as.list(.result))
  has_n <- any(vapply(nums, function(x) isTRUE(all.equal(sort(as.numeric(x)), c(120, 120))), logical(1)))
  right_mean <- any(vapply(nums, function(x) isTRUE(all.equal(sort(as.numeric(x)), target, tolerance = 1e-2)), logical(1)))
  any_na <- any(vapply(nums, function(x) any(is.na(x)), logical(1)))
  if (right_mean && has_n) {
    list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — 76.4 in the flipped arm against 70.7 in the traditional one, 120 students in each. You needed na.rm = TRUE to get there: without it, the eleven missing posttest scores turn both means into NA.")
  } else if (any_na) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "You got NA. Eleven students have no posttest score, and mean() of anything containing NA is NA. Add na.rm = TRUE inside mean() to average the students who do have a score.")
  } else if (right_mean) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "The means are right, but the count is missing. Add n = n() inside the same summarise().")
  } else if (has_n) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "The counts are right, but the means are not. You want mean(posttest, na.rm = TRUE) — check you are averaging posttest and not another column.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "Two things inside one summarise(): n = n() and mean_posttest = mean(posttest, na.rm = TRUE).")
  }
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_group"}
`group_by(teaching_arm)` first, then a single `summarise()` holding both
things, separated by a comma. `n()` takes no arguments; `mean()` takes the
column and then `na.rm = TRUE`.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 3: students per college"}
**Time:** 10 minutes

A stretch. Count how many students come from each `college`, with the
commonest college first. There are two good routes: `count()`, a shortcut you
have not met yet, or `group_by()` and `summarise()` followed by `arrange()`.
Either is a correct answer.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_college
students |>
  ______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_college
#| solution: true
students |>
  count(college, sort = TRUE)

# The long way round, using only the verbs above:
# students |>
#   group_by(college) |>
#   summarise(n = n()) |>
#   arrange(desc(n))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_college
#| check: true
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The answer should be a table with one row per college. count() and summarise() both give you one.")
} else if (!("college" %in% names(.result)) || nrow(.result) != 3) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Expected one row per college, and there are three colleges. Group or count by college, not by something else.")
} else {
  nums <- Filter(is.numeric, as.list(.result))
  counts <- if (length(nums) > 0) as.numeric(nums[[1]]) else numeric(0)
  if (identical(counts, c(89, 87, 64))) {
    list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — Thrissur 89, Kozhikode 87, Alappuzha 64, commonest first.")
  } else if (setequal(counts, c(89, 87, 64))) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "The counts are right but the order is not: you want the commonest first. Add sort = TRUE to count(), or pipe on into arrange(desc(n)).")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "You need a count column. Try count(college, sort = TRUE), or group_by(college) |> summarise(n = n()) |> arrange(desc(n)).")
  }
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_college"}
`count(college)` does the counting in one step and names the column `n`.
`sort = TRUE` puts the largest count at the top; without it you get the
colleges in alphabetical order.
:::
:::
